justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modestly bullish near-term bias anchored around the prevailing price level of SPY, which was trading in the low-to-mid 420s at the time of the forecast. For the one-day horizon, I anchored closely to the last observed price with only a small upward drift, reflecting the tendency of equity markets to have a slight positive bias on any given day but with very limited directional information available at that short horizon. For the one-week estimate, I added a slightly larger drift to account for the compounding of that daily positive bias, while still keeping the estimate close to spot given the lack of strong catalysts pulling strongly in either direction. For the one-month estimate, I extended the drift further, consistent with the long-run annualized return of the S&P 500 roughly translating into modest monthly gains, while acknowledging that a month is long enough for meaningful macro developments to shift the picture.

The confidence interval widths were calibrated using historical realized volatility of SPY as the primary input. At the one-day horizon, the interval is relatively tight because daily volatility for a broad index ETF like SPY is typically in the range of 0.5–1.5%, and absent a known high-impact event, the distribution of outcomes clusters fairly closely around the mean. At the one-week horizon, volatility scales with the square root of time, widening the interval meaningfully. By one month, the interval is quite wide, reflecting not just the mathematical scaling of volatility but also the growing probability that significant macro or geopolitical developments could emerge over a 30-day window that were entirely unpredictable at the time of the forecast.

Several specific risks could push outcomes outside my stated intervals. On the downside, an unexpected Federal Reserve policy shift, a sharp deterioration in economic data signaling recession, a credit event in the banking or commercial real estate sector, or an escalation of geopolitical conflict could plausibly send SPY well below 355 at the one-month horizon. On the upside, a surprisingly strong earnings season, a faster-than-expected disinflation path prompting rate cut expectations, or a significant positive resolution to a known geopolitical risk could push SPY above 510. At the one-day horizon, a surprise geopolitical shock or an unscheduled central bank announcement could easily breach the stated 405–442 range. These tail events are real but individually low-probability, which is why the intervals are designed to capture roughly 90% of plausible outcomes rather than 100%.
